# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about how we move through the world half-asleep, missing the extraordinary nature of completely ordinary things. This thought struck me while I was waiting in line at a coffee shop, watching the barista steam milk. The way the white liquid suddenly became a living thing—swirling, expanding, transforming into something entirely different from what it was moments before. It's pure alchemy, yet nobody pauses to marvel at it anymore.

We're all so busy chasing the spectacular that we've forgotten to notice what's already spectacular about simply existing.

Consider the human hand. Not in any mystical sense, but literally—that intricate arrangement of bones and muscles and tendons that lets you do virtually anything. The fact that your hand can write poetry, play piano, comfort someone in pain, or hold another person's hand in the dark. We take it for granted until we injure it, then suddenly we're furious at how much we depend on something we never consciously appreciated. But shouldn't we appreciate it anyway?

I think there's a particular kind of freedom in that realization. When you stop waiting for life to be interesting and start noticing that it already is, everything changes. Not in some transformative, movie-montage kind of way, but in small, genuine ways. A conversation with someone you've known for years becomes interesting again when you actually listen instead of planning what you'll say next. A walk becomes an adventure when you're not thinking about where you need to be. Your body becomes a miracle when you notice it breathing instead of resenting it for not looking like someone else's.

The difficult part—and maybe the most important part—is that this requires a kind of radical acceptance of things as they are. Our culture is built on the idea that things should be better, newer, faster, sexier. We're encouraged to always want more, to constantly improve ourselves, to never be satisfied. There's value in that drive, certainly, but there's also a particular kind of suffering built into it. You can always find ways that you don't measure up. There's always someone prettier, smarter, richer, more accomplished. The goalpost moves constantly.

But what if you just... stopped? What if you looked at your imperfect life and your imperfect self and decided it was enough? Not in a defeatist way, but in a generous way? I think that's where real peace lives.

I've noticed this in people who seem genuinely happy. They're not necessarily the most successful people, and they're definitely not the ones who have figured everything out. They're just the ones who seem comfortable in their own skin, who don't need to impress anyone, who can be interested in small things. My grandmother was like that. She'd spend an hour in her garden, genuinely delighted by the color of a tomato plant, the way a beetle looked in the sunlight. She had real problems, real struggles, but she also had that capacity for wonder that most of us lose somewhere between childhood and adulthood.

I think we lose it because we're taught that wonder is frivolous. That it's something you get to do after you've achieved important things. After you've gotten the job, the relationship, the money, the validation. But what if it's the other way around? What if wonder is the thing that makes the other stuff actually worth doing?

There's also something I've been thinking about regarding how connected we are to everything, even when we don't notice it. When you drink that coffee the barista made, you're consuming something that required sun and rain and soil and seeds and people harvesting beans and roasting them and countless decisions and efforts. The electricity that powered the espresso machine came from somewhere—maybe coal, maybe solar panels, maybe wind turbines spinning somewhere. The cup itself is made of ceramic, which requires clay and heat and more decisions. That coffee is a knot of the entire world tied together and placed in your hand for three dollars and fifty cents. How is that not miraculous?

We're all made of stardust, which is not just a poetic phrase but literally true. The iron in your blood was forged in the heart of a dying star. The calcium in your bones was made in supernovae. You are, quite literally, composed of the remnants of cosmic explosions. Your consciousness, that awareness looking out through your eyes right now, is somehow something that the universe has managed to do with itself. I don't understand it. Nobody really does. And yet we treat our existence like a commute—something to get through on the way to somewhere else.

Maybe the real rebellion against a hollow world is to insist on meaning in small moments. To notice things. To be present. To allow yourself to be delighted by a perfectly ripe peach, by the way light hits water, by a kind word from a stranger, by the fact that you're alive and aware and capable of experiencing anything at all.

I'm not saying you should quit your job and go live in the woods or stop having ambitions. But maybe the ambitions would mean more if they were grounded in actual presence, actual appreciation, actual awareness of what you're doing and why. Maybe you'd want different things if you weren't always running away from your own life and toward some imaginary future.

When I was young, I used to think that adults had figured something out, that there was some secret knowledge that would make everything click into place and then I'd finally be satisfied. Now I'm older and I realize the secret is that nobody figures it out. You just get better at noticing that you already have it. Whatever "it" is.

So here's what I want: I want to be the kind of person who notices the coffee being made. Who appreciates the hands that made it. Who tastes it like it's something worth tasting. Who looks at other people like they matter, because they do. Who can hold both ambition and contentment at the same time. Who doesn't need the world to be different in order to be grateful for it.

That seems like enough.
